paper_title: Editing Images into Reusable Layers via Compositional Edit-Prior Distillation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: High-quality image editing requires precise modification of target regions while preserving the content of unrelated regions. Existing editing models produce flattened outputs that limit precise local manipulation and layer reuse, while decomposition methods typically optimize layer recovery separately from instruction-driven editing. To this end, we introduce LayerEditor, a unified framework that couples instruction-guided image editing with controllable generation of reusable RGBA layers. At its core, In-Context RGB-Alpha Token Modeling jointly represents the edited canvas and an ordered sequence of RGB-Alpha layers within a single token sequence, enabling semantic edits and explicit control over individual layer content. To retain the pretrained model's editing capability during adaptation to layered outputs, we propose Compositional Edit-Prior Distillation, which transfers its editing prior to both the edited canvas and the image composed from the predicted layers. To support training and evaluation, we construct LayerEditor-100K, a large-scale paired image-editing dataset with ordered RGBA layer annotations, and introduce dedicated benchmarks for layered editing. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LayerEditor maintains strong editing fidelity while generating accurate RGBA layers, supporting both flexible layer-level manipulation and multi-layer decomposition.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Instruction-driven image editing aims to modify specified content while preserving unrelated regions of the source image. Recent editing models (Wu et al., 2025; Super Intelligence Team, 2026) commonly employ multimodal diffusion transformers to jointly model textual instructions and images within unified token sequence, synthesizing single flattened edited canvas in which text, objects, and background content are fused together. Such flattened outputs make it difficult to manipulate fine-grained details or incorporate detailed user-provided elements, which is crucial for downstream applications such as e-commerce content production and advertising design. Subsequent revisions therefore require repeated generation, increasing processing overhead and risking unintended changes to unrelated content and boundary artifacts. Image decomposition provides natural way to recover explicit layers from such flattened results (Yin et al., 2025; He et al., 2026; Tang et al., 2026). Decomposition and image editing can be combined into layered workflows, as illustrated by Agent Banana (Ye et al., 2026b). Yet editing and decomposition are typically optimized as separate stages with different objectives. Editing models focus on producing visually faithful results without considering the desired layer structure, while decomposition models recover layers after editing without jointly optimizing the requested edit and target layer structure. Consequently, even visually plausible edits may yield incomplete or poorly organized layers that are difficult to reuse. Moreover, directly extending pretrained editing model to layered outputs tends to degrade its original editing capability, i.e., the edited content exhibits quality drops or artifacts. To mitigate this degradation, we introduce on-policy Compositional Edit-Prior Distillation (C-EPD) which facilitates the models adaptation to layered outputs while maintaining its pre-trained generative editing capacity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LayerEditor preserves strong editing performance while supporting flexible layered outputs with variable layer counts and user-specified layer content. To further provide paired supervision for both editing outcomes and their underlying layer structures, we construct LayerEditor-100K, large-scale dataset tailored to instruction-driven layered image editing. Each example contains source image, editing instruction, edited target, and ordered RGBA layer stack, covering diverse text, object, and appearance edits with variable layer counts. In addition, since existing benchmarks do not adequately evaluate instruction-driven layered editing, we construct Crello-Testset and ScaleEdit-Testset, with dedicated settings for layer-count control and user-specified layer content, enabling systematic evaluation of editing fidelity, layer quality, and layered controllability. We introduce LayerEditor, unified model for editing images into reusable RGBA layers through In-Context RGBAlpha Token Modeling. LayerEditor supports variable layer counts and user-specified layer content. We construct LayerEditor-100K, large-scale dataset tailored to layered editing, containing annotated image pairs with ordered RGBA layers, together with two benchmarks, Crello-Testset and ScaleEdit-Testset, for evaluating layered editing quality and controllability. We propose C-EPD, an on-policy distillation strategy that transfers the pretrained editing prior to layered outputs, preserving editing fidelity during layered adaptation.

Related methods explored selective reconstruction, interactive control, and temporal consistency for more fine-grained manipulation (Wen et al., 2024; Xue et al., 2025; 2024). More recently, agentic systems extended image editing into multi-step planning and execution workflows. Visual ChatGPT (Wu et al., 2023) coordinated specialized visual tools through language-based planning, PhotoAgent (Yao et al., 2026) performed iterative aesthetic editing with search and visual feedback, and Agent Banana (Ye et al., 2026b) incorporated hierarchical planning and layer decomposition for localized editing. Despite improved editing quality and control, these approaches either produce flattened outputs or rely on cascaded workflows to recover editable layers.

sections.title: 2.2 LAYERED IMAGE GENERATION
sections.content: Existing layered visual modeling mainly focuses on layered generation and structured editing. LayerDiff (Huang et al., 2024), PSDiffusion (Huang et al., 2025), LayeringDiff (Kang et al., 2025), and LASAGNA (Yang et al., 2026) generate coordinated layers from text or spatial conditions. For graphic design, COLE (Jia et al., 2023), CreatiPoster (Zhang et al., 2025), and Editable Visual Design (Ye et al., 2026a) organize generated assets into editable structures, while MiLDEdit (Lin et al., 2026) and MRT (Tang et al., 2026) extend generation and editing to layered inputs. More recently, LaDe (Lungu-Stan et al., 2026) jointly generates design canvases and RGBA layers, and UniWorld-Design (Li et al., 2026b) supports layered generation and prompt-controlled decomposition. These methods emphasize layered generation and decomposition rather than jointly editing flattened source image and generating its edited layer stack. Image decomposition methods such as Qwen-Image-Layered (Yin et al., 2025) and LiWi (He et al., 2026) recover editable components from rendered images, with related transparency-aware methods improving opacity and boundary quality (Rhemann et al., 2009; Zhang & Agrawala, 2024; Yu et al., 2026). Decomposition is typically optimized separately from instruction-driven editing. LayerEditor addresses this gap by jointly editing flattened source image and generating the corresponding reusable RGBA layers. 2.3 ON-POLICY DISTILLATION On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers knowledge from teacher to student by querying the teacher online on states actually visited by the student. By supervising the students own trajectories, OPD reduces the mismatch between teacher-generated training data and the students evolving state distribution (Agarwal et al., 2024). Recent studies extended this idea to flow-based generative models. Flow-OPD (Fang et al., 2026) distilled specialized teachers through student rollouts and manifold anchoring, DiffusionOPD (Li et al., 2026a) studied continuous-state transition alignment, and STEPOPD (Wei et al., 2026) further explored extrapolated targets and intermediate representation alignment. Unlike progressive distillation (Salimans & Ho, 2022) and consistency models (Song et al., 2023), which mainly reduced the number of sampling steps, our goal is to preserve editing capability when extending pretrained editor from single-image outputs to structured layered outputs.

sections.title: 4.4 LAYER FIDELITY AND DECOMPOSITION CAPABILITY
sections.content: This section evaluates LayerEditor on pure image-to-layer decomposition, where the input image is preserved and only its reusable RGBA layers are recovered. We construct the benchmark from the original Crello test split by regrouping compatible native layers and retaining 1,171 held-out images with 210 reference layers. LayerEditor receives only the input image, preservation instruction, and the requested layer count, without I2L-specific fine-tuning or reference layer descriptions. We compare against QIL, QIL-Decomp-FT, and the iterative LayerD baseline (Suzuki et al., 2025), with evaluation details provided in Appendix C.2. LayerD follows its official inference procedure, with repeated decomposition to obtain the requested number of layers. As shown in Figure 6, LayerEditor achieves Composite SSIM of 0.8761, compared with 0.7963 for QIL. Its Alpha IoU of 0.6343 and layer-semantic score of 6.39 also exceed the corresponding QIL and QIL-Decomp-FT results. These observations support task transfer to image decomposition without I2L-specific fine-tuning. sections.title: SUPPLEMENTARY MATERIAL
sections.content: This supplementary material provides implementation details, dataset construction procedures, evaluation protocols, and additional experimental results. LayerEditor takes source image, requested layer count, and textual editing instruction that may additionally specify the desired content of individual layers. These textual conditions are used only as model inputs, while RGBA layers, Alpha masks, and related annotations serve exclusively as training supervision or evaluation references.

sections.content: Figure 8: LayerEditor-100K construction pipeline. Two complementary routes create editing pairs with reusable RGBA annotations from native designs and flattened editing pairs. Shared validation checks editing fidelity, layer quality, and reconstruction before export. LAYEREDITOR-100K CONSTRUCTION B.1 DATA CONSTRUCTION PIPELINE LayerEditor-100K combines two routes for obtaining paired editing supervision and reusable target layers (Figure 8). Every accepted record contains source image, instruction, edited target, and ordered full-canvas RGBA stack. Layer annotations provide RGBA supervision and aligned semantic descriptions for training the structured prompt interface (Appendix A.1). Route A: native layered designs. Crello and PrismLayersPro provide native assets with positions, stacking order, and transparency (Yamaguchi, 2021; Chen et al., 2025). We first render and consolidate the assets into 210 ordered layers, then plan the edit while keeping key text, subjects, and target regions separate where possible. Layout changes, movement, and deletion are handled deterministically, while generative editing is used for text redrawing, object replacement, and appearance modification. The edited content is finally combined with preserved RGBA layers to form the target stack, followed by semantic and visual quality verification. Route B: flattened editing pairs. ScaleEdit sourcetarget pairs (Chen et al., 2026) are screened for effective edits, readable content, and suitability for layered editing. planner proposes layer roles and granularity, and QIL (Yin et al., 2025) and Seedream5-Pro (ByteDance Seed, 2026) generate decomposition candidates. Candidates are standardized to full-canvas RGBA stacks with complete bottom background and transparent foreground support. Repairable failures receive at most two rounds of local correction for text defects, missing content, leakage, or Alpha artifacts, followed by full-stack review. Severe failures are rejected, and repairs are retained only when they improve the candidate. The original target is preserved when reconstruction passes. repaired composition becomes the target only after independent verification of instruction execution and content preservation. Both versions and the revision reason are retained. Benchmark construction. Crello-Testset and ScaleEdit-Testset are constructed separately from the native-design and flattened-pair source groups, with no training-source overlap. Their main editing results are evaluated separately. To construct the two controllability settings, we combine all samples from both benchmarks, modify the editing prompt or requested layer count, and revise each target and reference stack to match the modified request. Count-only changes regroup compatible Instruction changes update both edited layers while preserving the intended edited appearance. content and its reference layers. Each derived case fixes its source, conditions, target, and reference stack before inference. Target pixels and reference RGBA arrays are withheld from generation. Their annotations provide the supplied layer-content specifications.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Offline target-layer annotation and acceptance. Count and order: exactly nonempty layers in valid back-to-front order. Content isolation: complete intended components without duplication, cross-layer leakage, or unrelated background residue. Valid Alpha: transparent foreground support with appropriate continuous opacity at fine structures and semitransparent boundaries. Accurate recomposition: the stack reconstructs the target while retaining the requested edit and unchanged content. Record: layer index, role, visible content, edit status, and bounding box. Semantic descriptions support structured textual control. RGBA references and geometric metadata support supervision and validation. Figure 9: Offline layer annotation and quality criteria. Shared checks validate the target stack produced by either construction route. B.2 LAYER ANNOTATION AND QUALITY CONTROL Native layer metadata is updated after editing in Route A, while planner infers target-layer structure from the edited pair in Route B. Each layer is annotated with its index, role, content, edit status, and bounding box. Semantic roles and content descriptions populate the training prompt, while geometric metadata supports offline validation. Figure 9 summarizes the four acceptance conditions. Quality control follows common sequence of structure check, semantic check, layer QA, reconstruction, and deduplication. Structure checks validate count, dimensions, and order. Semantic checks compare source, instruction, and target, including transcription for text edits. Layer QA inspects isolated RGBA components and Alpha boundaries, and reconstruction checks compare the exact composition with the intended target. B.3 DATASET STATISTICS AND SPLIT LayerEditor-100K contains 100,000 accepted editing pairs from Crello, PrismLayersPro, and ScaleEdit. The dataset includes 48,329 text edits, 36,858 object edits, and 14,813 poster-level appearance edits, with 210 target layers per example. Counts refer to unique accepted records, excluding rejected candidates and repeated training exposures. Training and test documents do not overlap. All edits and layer organizations derived from the same source document remain in the same split. The original Crello documents used for I2L evaluation are also excluded from trainingdata construction. Crello-Testset contains 2,994 documents from native Crello and PrismLayersPro designs. ScaleEdit-Testset contains 1,000 documents from flattened ScaleEdit pairs with recovered layers. Layer-count control and instruction control are each evaluated on the combined full pool of 3,994 documents. In the layer-count setting, each source document typically yields two to four organizations at compact, intermediate, or detailed granularities. Each organization has corresponding count, ordered content description, and reference stack, with the source image and edited target preserved. The 3,994 count denotes source documents, not the number of derived requests. Scores are first averaged over the evaluated variants of each source document and then over source documents, so documents with more variants receive no additional weight. Instruction-control requests instead update the edited target and reference stack to match the new instruction. Layer-count results are reported in Table 2, and instruction-control results in Table 6. Every derived example remains in the test split of its source document.

sections.content: C.1 BASELINES Except for Seedream5-Pro, which is accessed through its hosted API, all baseline results are obtained from our own runs of the corresponding models. Pretrained or fine-tuned configurations are specified below. LayerD results in Figure 6 are also reproduced by us rather than taken from published tables. The FR editor in cascaded baselines is pretrained, whereas LayerEditor receives layered-editing adaptation. These are system-level comparisons and do not isolate joint modeling from editing-data

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: adaptation. Count-only baselines additionally differ in available conditions. Comparisons with QILControl, QIL-Edit-SFT, and Seedream5-Pro hold the supplied layer-content specifications fixed. Seedream5-Pro (Seq.). We access Seedream5-Pro through its API (ByteDance Seed, 2026). Seq. uses two calls: the first produces the edited image, and the second decomposes it using the requested count and layer-content descriptions. No task-specific fine-tuning is applied. Seedream5-Pro (Joint). Joint uses one API call with the source image, editing instruction, requested count, and the same layer-content descriptions supplied to LayerEditor. It requests editing and layer generation together. The returned stack supplies Composite outputs. No independent Direct canvas is exported in this setting. FR + QIL. FireRed edits the source, and pretrained QIL decomposes the result using the requested layer count (Super Intelligence Team, 2026; Yin et al., 2025). The FR stage uses 40 sampling steps, guidance of 4, and aspect-ratio-preserving dimensions aligned to multiples of 16 within 10242 pixel budget. All FR-based cascades reuse these edited canvases within each setting, including the supplementary instruction-control experiment. FR + QIL-Control. QIL-Control replaces QIL in the decomposition stage (DiffSynth-Studio Team, 2026). It uses text-conditioned extraction with the same ordered layer-content descriptions supplied to LayerEditor, and the requested count specifies the size of the assembled stack. No taskspecific fine-tuning is applied. QIL-Decomp-FT. QIL is fine-tuned on LayerEditor-100K targets and RGBA annotations following the official decomposition-training pipeline. It decomposes FR edits for layered editing or the source image for I2L, using the requested count without benchmark layer-content descriptions. QIL-Edit-SFT. This adapted QIL baseline learns canvas and layer generation directly from source images, editing instructions, requested counts, and layer-content descriptions. It uses the same content specifications as LayerEditor, with paired targets and RGBA stacks as supervision. RevealLayer. RevealLayer (Wang et al., 2026) decomposes the FR edit without task-specific finetuning. Its bounding-box guidance uses the benchmark reference annotations. The requested count guides repeated extraction and stack assembly, without benchmark layer-content descriptions. Postgeneration correspondence supports evaluation when the recovered organization differs from the reference. LayerD. LayerD (Suzuki et al., 2025) is included in the I2L comparison. We follow the official inference procedure and repeatedly invoke decomposition to assemble stack with the requested target layer count. These sequential calls incur substantial time cost as more layers are extracted. They are part of the decomposition pipeline, not single joint prediction of all layers. We use the pretrained model without task-specific fine-tuning. C.2 METRICS AND LAYER MATCHING Rendering and image metrics. Direct metrics compare the exported canvas with the target. sections.title: E LIMITATIONS
sections.content: LayerEditor is trained and evaluated with at most ten RGBA layers, leaving larger stacks unexplored. Thin structures, complex transparency, and semitransparent boundaries can still produce artifacts during layer movement or recomposition. Text remains rasterized rather than represented as editable font or vector primitives, limiting downstream typography manipulation. The current results do not establish lossless source reconstruction or artifact-free downstream reuse. Quantitative evaluation measures layer isolation, opacity, and recomposition in the evaluated layouts. We do not systematically test reconstruction after layer manipulation or validate VLM scores against human judgments. Editing-prior retention is evaluated on the constructed benchmarks rather than an independent general-editing test. Automatically constructed annotations and model-based assessments may contain errors and model-specific biases. Figure 11: Rubric score examples. For the same editing request, progressively improved outputs receive higher scores across editing fidelity, layer separation, composition, and Alpha quality. sections.title: F ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: LayerEditor enables instruction-driven image editing and reusable layered representations. As with other image editing systems, it may be misused to alter visual content deceptively or modify copyrighted assets without authorization. Our work is intended for research on controllable image editing and structured visual representations. LayerEditor-100K is constructed from existing research datasets and design resources, and we preserve source provenance throughout data processing. We do not intentionally collect additional private user information. Automated vision-language models are used for semantic verification and quality assessment, and we combine model-based evaluations with deterministic checks and structured quality-control procedures. Because layered outputs make subsequent visual manipulation easier, responsible deployment should consider content provenance, copyright, and safeguards against deceptive editing.
